q: A Client insists on knowing the total professional fee in full before construction starts, and by this point the scope of services — design, approvals, construction schedule — is already fully and clearly defined. Which compensation method should the Architect recommend?
o: Percentage-based Fee on PCC
Lump Sum or Fixed Fee
Multiple of Direct Personnel Expense
Per Diem, Honorarium plus Reimbursable Expenses
n: Lump Sum fits when scope, schedule, and approvals are already fully defined, letting both parties fix the total fee in advance.

q: A Client wants one party solely accountable for both the architectural design and the standard basic engineering disciplines (structural, plumbing/sanitary, mechanical, electrical). Under which contract type should the Architect be engaged?
o: Detailed Architectural Design Services (DADS)
Comprehensive Architectural Services
Detailed Architectural and Engineering Design Services (DAEDS)
Design-Build Services by Administration
n: DAEDS bundles architectural design with basic engineering under one contract, giving the Client a single point of responsibility.

q: An Architect is tasked with renovating the interior of an existing office, pricing the work against a comparable past project's unit cost per square meter. Relative to a new-build project priced at the same unit rate, how should the required service effort be regarded?
o: As equal, since the unit-cost method treats all projects the same way
As reduced, because renovation reuses existing structural elements
As greater, since renovation work demands more service effort per unit area than new work
As irrelevant, since the project should instead shift to a Lump Sum arrangement
n: The Guidelines explicitly note that renovation work demands more service effort per unit area than comparable new construction.

q: A Client needs the Architect to appear as an expert witness in a construction-related court proceeding — a brief, interim assignment that resists advance scoping. Which compensation method fits best?
o: Percentage of Gross Rentals
Unit Cost Method
Time Basis (hourly/per diem)
Value-based Pricing
n: Time Basis fits engagements that are short, interim, or hard to scope in advance, such as expert-witness testimony.

q: A Client wants an Architect on call for periodic consultation across the coming year — short of a full-time engagement — and is prepared to pay a fixed recurring amount for a minimum level of service. Which compensation arrangement suits this?
o: Multiple of Direct Personnel Expense
Retainer
Lump Sum or Fixed Fee
Value-based Pricing / Percentage of Gross Rentals
n: A Retainer is used precisely for on-call, interval-based engagements paid a regular stipulated amount for a minimum service obligation.

q: An architect's office is assigned purely clerical duties on a project — record-keeping, data collection, and report writing, with no creative design involved. Why does the Multiple of Direct Personnel Expense method suit this kind of task specifically?
o: It is the default for every service
It applies only when an engineer signs
Time spent can't measure creative value
It guarantees the highest possible fee
n: Multiple of DPE is reserved for non-creative work because time spent cannot fairly measure the value of creative design.

q: Within one project, an Architect is asked to produce marketing renderings (a clearly bounded, specific task) alongside ongoing design work for the rest of the project. How should compensation for these two components be structured?
o: Both parts as a percentage of PCC only
Renderings lump sum; the rest by another basis
Decline the renderings as outside the SPP
Both parts purely by the hour
n: Mixed Methods lets a determinate service be billed as a fixed price while other, less-determinate services use a different basis.

q: A Client commissions an Architect to design a public market featuring minimal architectural finishes and straightforward engineering needs. How should this project be classified under the Schedule of Fees?
o: Group 3 — exceptional character/complexity
Group 1 — simplest utilization/character
Group 5 — monumental buildings
Group 8 — extensive detail
n: Group 1 covers buildings with the simplest utilization/character and minimum finishes, such as public markets.

q: An Architect is hired to renovate and expand an existing school building, a structure originally falling under Group 2. How should the Recommended Professional Fee for this engagement be adjusted?
o: It stays the same, since the building type is unchanged
It is cut by half, since existing structural work is being reused
It rises by 50% — i.e., 150% of the applicable Group 9 (alterations/renovations) RPF
It is computed strictly on a Time Basis
n: Group 9 (alterations/renovations) adds 50% to the applicable RPF of the original building group, for a total of 150%.

q: Having finished the Detailed Design and Contract Documents Phase — representing 90% of the total work — the Architect then learns the Owner has decided to shelve the project. What is the Architect entitled to receive?
o: Only the fee for the Schematic Design Phase
90% of the total Professional Fee
The full 100% Professional Fee, regardless of how much was completed
No fee at all, since construction never began
n: Once the Contract Documents Phase (90% of work) is done, the Architect keeps 90% of the fee even if the Owner abandons the project.

q: Unforeseen circumstances halt the Construction Phase of a project for eight months. Once work resumes, how should the fee for the remaining Periodic Construction Supervision work be treated?
o: Unchanged from what was originally agreed
Cut in half to reflect the delay
Doubled, since the suspension ran past six months
Automatically converted into a Lump Sum arrangement
n: A construction suspension beyond six months doubles the fee for the remaining Periodic Construction Supervision work.

q: A Client opts to engage a Specialist Consultant directly and separately rather than through the Architect, yet still expects the Architect-of-Record to coordinate that consultant's work with the overall design. What compensation does the Architect earn for this coordination effort?
o: None — coordination is already covered by the basic fee
A coordination fee equal to 5% of the Specialist Consultant's fee
Half of the Specialist Consultant's fee
A fee matching the SC's fee in full, paid by the Client
n: When a Client engages a Specialist Consultant directly, the Architect-of-Record still earns a 5% coordination fee on the SC's fee.

q: An Architect and Client disagree over the terms of a Service Agreement. Fourteen calendar days of direct negotiation pass without resolution. What should happen next, before formal arbitration begins?
o: Filing a case at once in a regular court
Mediation with a neutral party for 14 days
The Architect terminates the agreement
Waiting until the Client agrees to arbitrate
n: Sec. 19.2 sequences dispute resolution: negotiation first, then mediation with a neutral third party, before formal arbitration.

q: An Owner leaves the Architect's billed fees unpaid for thirty days after receiving the statement of account, with no dispute as to the amount owed. What does the Architect become entitled to under the Guidelines?
o: Nothing, since fees are only due upon project completion
Interest at the prevailing BSP rate, as mutually agreed with the Client
Automatic termination of the Service Agreement
A penalty equal to half the unpaid amount
n: Sec. 16 entitles the Architect to interest at the BSP rate on fees unpaid 30 days after billing, as agreed with the Client.

q: An unlicensed, unregistered individual accepts payment for architectural design services performed on a residential project. How does the UAP fee guideline characterize that act?
o: Permissible, so long as the Client consents in writing
Permissible only for Group 4 (residential) projects
Unlawful, as provided under R.A. 9266
Permissible if a licensed Architect subsequently reviews the work
n: R.A. 9266 makes it unlawful for anyone without a valid license/registration to collect fees for architectural services.
